c.tagline: Haiti's colonial second city, gateway to the mountaintop Citadelle and Sans-Souci Palace.

taxi.fareNote: There are no ride-hailing apps; getting around means shared tap-taps (converted pickups on fixed routes) and moto-taxis, or a private car hired through your hotel. Fares are unmetered and negotiated first — US dollars are accepted almost everywhere alongside the gourde.

emergency.note: Formal emergency services are limited and many visitors rely on their hotel or a private driver; check your government's current Haiti travel advisory before going.

avoid.reason: Avoid all road travel toward Port-au-Prince and isolated areas outside the city; while Cap-Haïtien is calmer than the capital, check current security conditions as gang activity fluctuates.
Petty theft occurs in the Marché de Fer market area and crowded streets — keep valuables out of sight and avoid walking after dark.

hood_desc: Cap-Haïtien's tightly gridded colonial core around the Place d'Armes and the twin-towered Notre-Dame Cathedral, full of gingerbread balconies, the Iron Market, and street life; the walkable base for most visitors.
The breezy seafront district along the Boulevard du Carénage, where locals stroll, eat, and watch the harbour; a lively, central place to stay near the water.
A sprawling, densely populated fishing and residential zone east of the centre across the bay; authentic and local, with few tourist services.
The city's southern gateway rising toward Fort Vertières, monument to the 1803 battle that sealed Haiti's independence; mostly residential and historically significant rather than touristy.
The resort-and-beach coast west of town toward Labadie, home to Cormier Plage and quiet cove hotels; a relaxed seaside base away from the city bustle.

water.note: Drink only bottled or treated water; cholera outbreaks have occurred.

transit.hours: Tap-taps and moto-taxis run through daylight and into the evening; service thins after dark.
transit.note: Cap-Haïtien has no formal bus or rail network. Shared tap-taps (brightly painted pickups on fixed routes) and moto-taxis are the everyday transport, alongside private hired cars.
transit.pay: Pay the driver in cash — gourdes or US dollars — as you get off a tap-tap (a few gourdes per hop); moto-taxi and private fares are negotiated first.

bus: Tap-tap shared taxis around the city
Long-distance buses and vans to Port-au-Prince via national highways
ferry: Occasional coastal boats to Labadie and nearby beaches

transit.m: Taxi or hotel shuttle to the city centre (10-15 min)

tip.r: ~10% at restaurants where service isn't already added; small tips to guides and drivers are appreciated.
